rewrites.summary:
No criminal exposure: the territory's own legislature decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 1979 code revision (effective 1980), age of consent equal at 16. No local protections of practical substance exist: nothing criminalises a trans visitor, and next to nothing shields one.

Partner travel is the sharpest edge. Marriages performed elsewhere must be recognised under a 2022 federal statute, yet the territory performs none: officials long treated the 2015 federal ruling as 'under review', a judge said in 2016 he would not apply it, and licences remain withheld through 2024-26 — a 2026 review concludes any same-sex applicant must be served, but none has applied, so on-island spousal recognition is untested.

Social climate is conservative and church-centred, reserved behaviour expected; yet it is the homeland of a widely accepted indigenous third-gender presence; trans-presenting travellers more often meet cultural familiarity than the hostility recorded in some neighbouring islands. Net: low state risk, thin institutional cover, reliance on informal tolerance.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Applicability of the 2015 federal marriage-ruling remains formally unsettled on-island — the territory's attorney general said in 2015 it was 'still being reviewed'; a district-court judge confirmed in 2016 he had not read it and would not perform such weddings absent local law change. A 2026 practitioners' review argues the ruling binds, but reaching that conclusion runs through the territorial high court and then the federal department overseeing territories — a path no one has taken.

Nothing newer than 2024-26: no post-2024 territorial ruling, law or incident touching trans people was located, and a 2024 on-island legal survey still treats the local marriage restriction as operative and its constitutional durability as open.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Fa'afafine — raised male, embodying both genders — are documented as integral to traditional Samoan family life; the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa formed in 2010 as explicit cultural reclamation, and at the 2003 senate hearing fa'afafine witnesses themselves opposed the marriage bill on cultural and religious grounds. Birth-record gender markers change only with medical documentation; plain corrections are limited to record errors.

A 2024 on-island survey by a visiting constitutional-law professor tested whether the marriage ban would survive a 14th-Amendment challenge, framing local culture in collectivist terms — a residents' and scholars' debate with little direct visitor stake.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: US passport 'X' marker availability for ASM-linked nationals is unverified. No trans-specific incident or enforcement episode for 2024-26 was found; absence of evidence is not safety. Comparative-ranking language is out of scope for this record.
rewrites.blindSummary:
A South Pacific island territory of a large federal republic, partly under chiefly customary governance. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised by the local legislature in a 1979 code revision effective 1980, age of consent equal at 16; there are no local non-discrimination protections of practical substance. A trans visitor meets a state that neither criminalises nor defends them.

Partner recognition rests on a 2022 federal statute covering unions performed elsewhere, but the territory performs none itself, officials have treated the 2015 federal ruling as unsettled since 2015, and licences remain withheld in practice; a 2026 review says applicants must be served, yet none has applied, so on-the-ground spousal recognition is untested.

Social climate is conservative and faith-centred, with reserve expected; an indigenous third-gender role is long accepted and locally visible, so trans-presenting travellers may meet cultural familiarity rather than the hostility of some neighbouring jurisdictions. Low state risk, thin institutional cover, informal tolerance load-bearing.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The federal marriage ruling's local applicability is formally unsettled: a 2015 official said it was 'under review' and a 2016 judicial confirmee said his court would not apply it absent local change; a 2026 practitioners' review says it binds, but enforcement would run through a two-tier court ladder no one has climbed.

Dated, not current: the freshest jurisdiction-specific sources stop at 2024-26; no newer ruling, law or incident was found.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
An indigenous third-gender social role, raised male and embodying both genders, is described as integral to traditional family life; a cultural-reclamation society for it formed in 2010, and its members themselves opposed the 2003 marriage bill at a legislative hearing. Birth-register gender markers change only with medical documentation.

A 2024 on-island survey examined whether the marriage restriction survives the federal constitution's equal-protection test — a residents' debate.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Gender-marker ('X') passport availability for this territory's federal nationals is unverified. No 2024-26 incident record found; absence of evidence is not safety. Ranking language prohibited.
blindSourceSummaries: University research guide (updated 2026) with substantive territory content: the indigenous third-gender community formally organised in 2010 as cultural reclamation; colonial suppression followed by reclaiming of local gender identities.

Travel column (2009): a traditional, reserved society where homosexuality is described as widely accepted in local culture, unlike a neighbouring island nation known for hostility; hotels skew toward business travel.

News report (2015): the federal marriage-equality ruling's applicability to this unincorporated territory was left 'under review' while all peer territories moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made; experts warned the review had a chilling effect.

2003 report: the territory's upper legislative chamber voted down a bill outlawing same-sex marriages before any US state ruling forced the question; gender-variant residents testified they sought no such marriages.

2016 report: a unanimously confirmed former territory attorney general, seated as a district judge, said he had not read the US marriage-equality ruling, that his court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and he would not perform same-sex weddings unless laws changed.

2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in the territory: the federal ruling does bind the territory and marriage certificates must be issued to any same-sex couple applying; to date none has applied; litigation route (territorial high court, then the federal department for territories) set out but untested.

2024 on-island survey of a constitutional-law question: nine years after the federal ruling and after a 2022 federal recognition mandate, the local ban is treated as operative on-island and its constitutional durability as an open question.
